topic: The first human-to-human heart transplant was performed by Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, South Africa, on 3 December 1967 (a Sunday, in the early hours); the patient, Louis Washkansky, lived 18 days before dying of pneumonia (Britannica 'Christiaan Barnard'; Heart of Cape Town Museum). American surgeons Norman Shumway and Richard Lower had developed the technique in hundreds of dog experiments at Stanford; Shumway performed the first US adult heart transplant on 6 January 1968 (Britannica; NIH/NLM). Median survival after heart transplant is now about 12–13 years (ISHLT registry; Cleveland Clinic). Roughly 6,000 heart transplants are performed worldwide each year (GODT/WHO; ISHLT).
policy_note: Every spoken or shown fact → a claim with ≥ 2 independent publishers; core claims need a primary/scholarly source.

myths.myth: The first heart transplant was American — the technique was invented at Stanford.
myths.reality: The technique was largely developed in the US, but the first human operation was done in Cape Town, South Africa, on 3 December 1967, a month before the first US adult transplant.

landscape.our_gap: First-heart-transplant clips are biography pieces about the surgeon; nobody puts the operation on a map at the far end of Africa, splits 18 days against 12 years, and counts the yearly transplants as a quiz.
